questions.q: Quantitative data is
questions.why: Quantitative = numbers; qualitative = words and meanings.

questions.q: A sample that represents the population is
questions.why: Representativeness allows generalisation.

questions.q: Positivists prefer
questions.why: Interpretivists prefer qualitative methods.

questions.q: A researcher lets 20 unemployed people talk freely in long, unstructured interviews about their experiences. What is the main strength of this method?
o: High reliability, because it is easy to repeat exactly
High validity, because it gives rich, detailed data in people's own words
The results can easily be generalised to the whole population
The data is quick to turn into statistics
questions.why: Unstructured interviews produce in-depth qualitative data that reflects respondents' real meanings, so validity is high; small samples and lack of standardisation weaken reliability and generalisation.

questions.q: A researcher picks every 10th name from a school register to build a sample. Which sampling method is this?
questions.why: Systematic sampling chooses people at a fixed interval from a sampling frame, such as every 10th name.

long.q: Describe two advantages of using questionnaires in sociological research.
scheme: B1: one advantage, e.g. large samples can be reached quickly and cheaply
B1: developed: so results can be generalised
B1: a second advantage, e.g. standardised questions give reliable, comparable data
B1: developed: easy to analyse statistically

questions.q: Norms are
questions.why: Norms guide everyday behaviour.

questions.q: Primary socialisation mainly takes place in
questions.why: In early childhood, within the family.

questions.q: What are norms?
questions.why: Values are beliefs about what is important.

questions.q: A boy is told 'boys don't cry' and given toy cars, while his sister is given dolls and praised for being gentle. What does this illustrate?
o: Secondary socialisation by the peer group
Gender role socialisation in the family
questions.why: Parents are teaching different expected behaviours to boys and girls during primary socialisation, which is gender role socialisation.

questions.q: A group of young people share their own music, clothes and slang but still accept most of society's main values. This group is best described as…
questions.why: A subculture has some distinctive norms and values within the wider culture; a counter-culture actively rejects mainstream values.

long.q: Describe two ways in which the peer group socialises young people.
scheme: B1: one way, e.g. peer pressure encourages conformity to group norms (dress, music, language)
B1: developed: those who don't conform face informal sanctions such as teasing or exclusion
B1: a second way, e.g. peers act as role models for attitudes and behaviour
B1: developed: this shapes identity, e.g. through youth subcultures

questions.q: Social mobility means
questions.why: Upward or downward mobility.

questions.q: A meritocracy is a system where rewards are based on
questions.why: Functionalists claim modern societies are meritocratic.

questions.q: What is social mobility?
o: Movement of people between social classes
Changing jobs at the same level
questions.why: It can be upward or downward, within or between generations.

questions.q: The daughter of a factory worker becomes a doctor. What type of social mobility is this?
questions.why: Her position is compared with her parent's, across generations, and she has moved to a higher-status occupation.

questions.q: Which is an example of relative poverty rather than absolute poverty?
o: A family lacks enough food to stay healthy
A family has no access to clean drinking water
A family cannot afford the school trips and holidays that most families in their society take
questions.why: Relative poverty is judged against the normal living standards of a society; the other options describe a lack of basic needs, which is absolute poverty.

long.q: Explain two ways in which social class can affect a person's life chances.
scheme: B1: one way, e.g. health: working-class people tend to have lower life expectancy
B1: developed: e.g. poorer housing and diet, less access to private healthcare
B1: a second way, e.g. education: middle-class children are more likely to reach university
B1: developed: e.g. cultural capital, paying for tutors, or moving near high-performing schools

questions.q: A nuclear family consists of
questions.why: The extended family includes wider kin.

questions.q: What is a nuclear family?
o: Two parents and their dependent children
questions.why: The extended family includes other relatives.

questions.q: Which is evidence of family diversity?
o: Growth of single-parent and same-sex families
questions.why: Explain why the change has happened.

questions.q: Two divorced parents remarry and live together with the children from both of their previous marriages. What type of family is this?
questions.why: A reconstituted (blended) family is formed when adults with children from earlier relationships form a new household.

questions.q: Which is a likely reason for the rise in divorce rates in many societies?
o: Women becoming more financially dependent on men
Laws making divorce easier and cheaper to obtain
questions.why: Legal changes have lowered the cost and difficulty of divorce; the other options would make divorce less likely.

long.q: 'The nuclear family is no longer the main family type.' Evaluate this view. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: for: growth of lone-parent families, e.g. through divorce or choice
B1: for: other diverse types, e.g. reconstituted, same-sex, cohabiting, single-person households
B1: for: supported with a theorist or trend, e.g. the Rapoports on family diversity
B1: against: most people still live in a nuclear family at some stage of life
B1: against: e.g. Chester's 'neo-conventional family': the nuclear form has adapted rather than disappeared
B1: a reasoned judgement that follows from the points made

questions.q: The 'hidden curriculum' is
o: the values and attitudes learned informally at school
questions.why: e.g. punctuality, obedience.

questions.q: What is the hidden curriculum?
o: Values and attitudes taught informally through school life
questions.why: For example punctuality and obedience.

questions.q: How might material deprivation affect educational achievement?
o: Lack of resources such as books, space or food can lower attainment
questions.why: Cultural factors and labelling in school also matter.

questions.q: A teacher expects a pupil to do badly, gives them less attention, and the pupil's work gets worse. What concept describes this?
questions.why: The teacher's label shapes how the pupil is treated, and the pupil comes to live up to the prediction.

questions.q: Middle-class parents use their knowledge of how schools work to choose the best school and help with homework. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.why: Cultural capital is the knowledge, attitudes and skills, often passed on by middle-class families, that give children an advantage in education.

long.q: Explain why girls have tended to outperform boys at school in many countries.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. changing employment opportunities and aspirations for women
B1: developed: girls see qualifications as the route to a career (e.g. Sharpe's study of girls' changing priorities)
B1: a second reason, e.g. boys' anti-school or 'laddish' subcultures
B1: developed: being seen to work hard is 'uncool', so boys put in less effort

questions.q: Deviance is
o: behaviour that goes against social norms
questions.why: Deviance need not be criminal.

questions.q: Formal social control includes
questions.why: Informal control comes from family, peers and community.

questions.q: What is deviance?
o: Behaviour that goes against a society's norms
questions.why: Not all deviance is criminal.

questions.q: What is the dark figure of crime?
o: Crime that is not reported or recorded
questions.why: So official statistics are incomplete.

questions.q: A teenager is called a 'troublemaker' by teachers and police, starts to see himself that way, and commits more crime. Which explanation fits best?
o: Labelling leading to a self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.why: Interactionists argue that a label can change a person's self-image so that they act out the label, increasing deviance.

long.q: Explain why some social groups appear more often in official crime statistics.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. police target certain groups (labelling, stereotyping)
B1: developed with how this raises recorded crime
B1: a second reason, e.g. material deprivation or subcultures
B1: developed with a link to evidence or a theorist

questions.q: A 'moral panic' is
o: an exaggerated public reaction to a group seen as a threat
questions.why: Cohen's study of Mods and Rockers.

questions.q: What is a moral panic?
o: Exaggerated media reaction to a group seen as a threat
questions.why: Cohen's folk devils.

questions.q: What is agenda-setting by the media?
o: Choosing which issues the public thinks about
questions.why: Gatekeepers decide what is reported.

questions.q: The owners of a newspaper make sure it never criticises their other businesses or their political allies. Which view of the media does this support?
questions.why: Marxists argue that powerful owners control media content to protect their own interests and ideas.

questions.q: Teenagers say they watch a talent show so they can relax and chat about it with friends the next day. Which model of media effects does this support?
questions.why: The uses and gratifications model sees audiences as active, choosing media to meet their own needs such as relaxation and social interaction.

long.q: Describe how the media can create a moral panic.
scheme: B1: exaggerated or sensationalised reporting of a group or event
B1: the group is labelled as 'folk devils', a threat to society's values
B1: public concern grows and moral entrepreneurs demand action, e.g. tougher laws or policing
B1: an example or theorist, e.g. Cohen's study of Mods and Rockers
